source.title: Reinforcement Unlearning via Group Relative Policy Optimization
source.authors: Efstratios Zaradoukas; Bardh Prenkaj; Gjergji Kasneci

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a new GRPO-based unlearning method and reports its performance on adversarial prompts and forgetting measures, bearing on whether prompting can elicit targeted knowledge after unlearning.
record.gate_note: The reported RWKU AA results and the explicit 8-of-9 robustness statement are included. Figure 4 shows separate attack-type results, but the extracted text does not provide their individual numeric values. The discussion's uncertainty about representational erasure is a caveat, not a test of activation-direction ablation or evidence that PURGE blocks access rather than deletes knowledge. Cited results from prior work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study proposes a new unlearning method, PURGE (GRPO with a binary forbidden-entity reward). It measures the target knowledge left after unlearning on the RWKU Famous People set (FB, QA and the nine-attack AA split, as ROUGE-L recall) and general utility on Phi-3-Mini-4K-Instruct, against the intact model and five baselines it runs itself. This bears on F (a newer method claims to resist the attacks) and on A (forgetting depth with general ability kept, and attacks not recovering the knowledge). It runs no fine-tuning, internal-edit or quantization attack. The prompt attacks are compared only with the intact model, and the un-attacked splits use different questions, so prompt-based recovery (E) is not isolated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim PURGE gives verifiable, token-efficient unlearning (up to 46x fewer tokens per target), about 11% unlearning effectiveness with about 98% of utility kept, the best fluency, and +12% adversarial robustness over the base model (robust on 8 of 9 attacks). They concede that the reward works at the level of surface token suppression and that internal erasure is unverified. They also report that larger Qwen-2.5 models retain the target more stubbornly.
record.recipe_differences: PURGE uses GRPO with a binary forbidden-entity reward and a synthetic forget corpus built from model probes and extracted entities; it does not use the recovery attacks specified in the claim. The study also compares against GA, DPO, NPO, RT, and ICU.
record.method_sensitivity: The AA ROUGE-L result varies with the NER-constructing LLM used to build the synthetic forget corpus (.397 to .558 in Table 3).
record.problems: The AA analysis lacks a matched un-attacked comparison and a model retrained without target knowledge. The reported main forget metric is ROUGE-L recall, not an accuracy measure with a stated chance level. Figure 4's attack-specific values are not available numerically in the extracted text, and the paper does not identify the one attack outside its 8-of-9 robustness statement.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 4's separate values for each method and attack type are not extracted because the text does not provide their numbers; the aggregate 8-of-9 PURGE statement is retained in r8. Figure 3's Qwen-2.5 size-scaling plots and their utility metrics are omitted because the plotted values are not available numerically in the text and do not test recovery attacks. Neighbor-set, MIA, token-budget, and other utility results are outside the claim versions recorded here.

untested.parts: The clause that simple attacks don't recover the knowledge is tested only with RWKU prompt attacks: no fine-tuning, ablation or quantization. ROUGE-L recall has no chance level, and no model retrained without the target is compared (RWKU setting).
No relearning or fine-tuning recovery attack.
No activation-direction ablation or representational analysis. The authors only state that it is unclear whether the knowledge is erased or suppressed.

The nine RWKU attacks are run, but Table 1 and Figure 4 compare attacked scores only with the intact model. The un-attacked FB and QA splits use different questions, so whether prompting restores suppressed knowledge is not isolated. In an unmatched comparison, PURGE keeps 80% of BASE on AA and 81% on QA.
Robustness is tested only against RWKU prompt attacks. There are no fine-tuning, ablation or quantization attacks, and per-attack numbers are not reported.

missing.what: Un-attacked forget-set ROUGE-L for the baselines. Examples: NPO FB .296 and QA .257 vs BASE .483 and .523; GA QA .488; DPO QA .516; RT QA .479; ICU QA .514. These are needed to judge each baseline's forgetting apart from the AA split, and for the unmatched AA-vs-QA comparison.
missing.locator: Table 1, Forget Set FB and QA columns, rows ICU/GA/DPO/NPO/RT

record.verdict_notes:
All 23 rows in the record carry the undeclared ids V1-V6. Each row now has exactly one row_fixes item with declared ids, decided from what the row measures: V1 maps to A (forgetting/utility), V6 to F (PURGE's robustness claim), and V5 (E) is dropped because no row isolates prompt-based recovery. V2-V4 are on no row.

Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) r6 (RT) changed from absent to partial: −4.5 AA points, consistent with small FB/QA drops. RT moves from the A 'challenges' label (now GA and DPO only) to the A 'limits_scope' baseline label.
(2) Added an untested entry for A: only prompt attacks, and no chance-level or retrained reference.
(3) Added a missing entry for the baselines' un-attacked FB/QA values in Table 1.
(4) Rewrote the E untested text. Table 1 does give un-attacked scores, but on different questions; the unmatched AA/QA retention for PURGE is 80% vs 81%.
(5) Softened r15's attribution of the abstract's '11%'.
(6) Expanded r21-r23 on the likely swapped TOFU columns. If they are swapped, PURGE's forget-quality p-value of 1.1e-19 means little forgetting toward the retrained model.
(7) r16 now notes that PURGE has the largest MMLU drop of any method.
(8) Added the Qwen scale point to authors_conclusion.

The other judgments are kept. The 'robustness' claim compares attacked outputs with the intact model, not with the unlearned model's own un-attacked answers, so it shows weak forgetting that holds under attack rather than resistance to recovery. In Appendix F's qualitative examples, a synonym-manipulation prompt makes PURGE output 'Stephen King' itself (the forget target). Figure 3 (Qwen) and the Figure 4 per-attack values are declared in rows_left_out. The study is not an original source. No instructions addressed to the reader were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports forgetting and utility measures, but does not establish that targeted-knowledge accuracy reaches chance; its forget measures are ROUGE-L recall, and no chance-level reference is stated. The AA results do not compare attacked prompts with matched un-attacked prompts or a model retrained without the target knowledge.
No recovery fine-tuning attack using unrelated, loosely related, or selected forgotten facts is reported.
No activation-direction ablation or internal-edit recovery test is reported.

The paper tests the RWKU adversarial-attack prompt split, including cross-lingual and in-context-learning patterns, but not every possible rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or prompt-only recovery strategy. It lacks a matched un-attacked comparison and a model retrained without the target knowledge.
PURGE is evaluated against the RWKU adversarial-prompt attacks, not against fine-tuning, activation ablation, or quantization attacks.

rows.operation_detail: TOFU Forget Quality evaluation after PURGE
rows.measure: Forget Quality; closer to 1 indicates stronger forgetting
rows.note: The authors describe PURGE as competitive on TOFU, but give no chance-level or retrained-model reference.
rows.check: TOFU Table 2 (Llama-3.2-1B) appears to be column-confused. In the third column 'Retain' = 1 and the other values are p-value-like (1e-22 to 1e-6), as Forget Quality is. statements.correction: PURGE on Phi-3-Mini-4K-Instruct (3.8B), RWKU Famous People: AA forget ROUGE-L recall .481±.174 vs BASE .601±.172 (−12.02 points). The authors report robustness on 8 of 9 attack types (Figure 4, differences from base; the exception is not named, no numbers). Residual overlap stays substantial, but the method partly resists, so it limits F rather than challenging it.
statements.problem: The statement gives no number or claim for this study, yet it cites r7 and r8 as 'challenges' evidence against F. PURGE is a counter-method that partly resists the RWKU attacks, which fits limits_scope for F (as verdict l3 says), not challenges. The AA split has no matched un-attacked set for the unlearned model. The conditions list ('3B-8B Llama, Mistral, Tiny Aya and diffusion LMs') leaves out this study's model, Phi-3-Mini-4K-Instruct.
